stage1.probe_response: From the sensor data (notably the negative z‐displacement at only small forward motion and the high force readings), the scraper is binding mechanically, not just overcoming sticky residue. In other words, the wide scraper blade is being wedged between the raised grill ridges and the side walls, forcing it downward into the gaps. Increasing the Y‐axis push only drives the tool more firmly into that wedged position. To resolve this, the tool’s orientation or path must be changed so it does not bridge (and therefore jam against) the ridges, rather than simply increasing straight‐ahead force.

tool_selection.full_response:
Several factors stand out:

• The grill surface is both sticky and uneven (due to its parallel gaps).  
• The scraper is much wider than the individual gaps, creating a geometry mismatch that requires attention to orientation and force distribution.  
• The side walls constrain lateral movement and can guide the scraper, but they also limit angled approaches.  
• The sensor data shows that moderate force (85 N) barely moved the scraper across the sticky surface, while a higher force (150 N) pushed it slightly further. This confirms we need sufficient force to shear off the residue without causing structural damage.   
• We only get one attempt: the single-shot push must be precise in both angle and force.  

The uniqueness lies in the deep parallel gaps of the grill combined with a rigid, wide scraper, and the fact that the surface is coated with sticky residue requiring substantial force. Additionally, the side walls can help guide the scraper, but if we push incorrectly, we risk jamming or bending the scraper (or the grill).  

Given this scenario, the best tool to solve the task is the scraper.
